paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Long before electric air conditioning was invented, people living in the hot, dry regions of the Middle East had found a way to keep their homes cool without burning any fuel. Their solution was the windcatcher, a tall tower rising above the roof of a building and open near the top on one or more sides. Known in Persian as the badgir, the windcatcher became a defining feature of desert towns across Iran and the shores of the Persian Gulf. The central Iranian city of Yazd, where hundreds of these towers still stand, is often called the city of windcatchers. Historians are not certain when the first towers were built, but similar roof structures appear in paintings of Egyptian houses made more than three thousand years ago.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A windcatcher works by exploiting two simple physical principles. The first is the pressure of moving air. When the wind strikes the open side of a tower, the air is forced down a vertical shaft and into the rooms below. As this fresh air enters the house, it pushes warmer, stale air out through doors and windows on the opposite side. The second principle comes into play when there is no wind at all. Because warm air is lighter than cool air, it naturally rises. On still days, air that has been heated inside the house drifts up the tower and escapes from the top, drawing cooler air in at ground level to replace it. This process is known as the stack effect, and it means that a well-designed tower continues to ventilate a building even in calm weather.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Over the centuries, builders added several refinements to make the system more effective. Inside the tower, the shaft was usually divided by thin walls into a number of separate channels, so that air arriving from one direction could descend through one channel while warm air left through another. The towers themselves were generally built of thick mud brick, a material that absorbs heat slowly during the day and releases it at night. In some houses, the incoming air was led across a shallow pool or past porous clay jars filled with water. As the water evaporated, it absorbed heat from the air, lowering its temperature by several degrees. The most sophisticated designs connected the tower to a qanat, an underground channel that carried water from distant hills, so that air was cooled as it passed over the flowing water deep beneath the building.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The shape and height of windcatchers varied considerably from place to place. In areas where the wind blew mainly from one direction, a tower open on a single side was sufficient. Where the wind was less predictable, builders preferred towers with four or even eight openings, so that at least one would always face the breeze. Height mattered too. Air moves faster further above the ground and carries less dust, so taller towers delivered stronger and cleaner airflow. In wealthy households, the height and decoration of a windcatcher also served as a visible sign of the owner's status.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: During the twentieth century, many windcatchers fell into disrepair. Electric fans and, later, mechanical air conditioning offered a more convenient way to stay cool, and new buildings were rarely designed with towers. Yet mechanical cooling comes at a considerable cost. According to Dr Leila Farahani, an energy analyst at the Institute for Desert Architecture, air conditioning now accounts for a large share of summer electricity demand in many hot countries. The units themselves also release heat into the surrounding streets, which makes cities even warmer and increases the demand for cooling still further.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Concerns of this kind have led to renewed interest in the old technology. In 2019, an engineering team led by Professor Martin Okafor at the University of Carran fitted a modern windcatcher to a two-storey office building. Their tower was made of lightweight aluminium rather than brick, and its openings were fitted with movable louvres that a computer opened and closed according to the direction of the wind. Sensors measured the temperature inside the building, and whenever it rose too high, a fine mist of water was sprayed into the shaft to cool the incoming air. Over two summers, the team found that the building needed mechanical cooling on only a quarter of the days on which it would normally have been switched on.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Okafor admits that windcatchers are not suitable everywhere. They work best in dry climates, because evaporative cooling is far less effective when the air is already humid. They are also difficult to add to tall apartment blocks, where air would have to travel long distances through the building. Nevertheless, he believes that the principle behind the towers deserves far wider attention. 'For centuries, builders understood how to work with the climate rather than against it,' he says. 'Modern engineering has a great deal to learn from them.'

passage.title: The puzzle of the dawn chorus

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who wakes before sunrise in a temperate woodland in spring will hear it: a swelling wave of birdsong that begins in near-darkness, reaches a peak around first light and fades within an hour or two. The dawn chorus is one of the most familiar events in the natural world, yet it has proved surprisingly difficult to explain. Singing is not free. It consumes energy, it takes time that could otherwise be spent feeding, and it can reveal a bird's position to predators. Why, then, do so many species concentrate their most intense singing into the hour when they are hungriest after a long night without food? Over the past half-century, biologists have proposed a range of answers, and the debate is still far from settled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the earliest explanations focused on the physics of sound. At dawn the air is usually cool and still, without the turbulence that develops later in the day as the sun heats the ground. In theory, these conditions should allow songs to travel further and remain clearer over distance. The ornithologist Harriet Vance, working in English beech woods in the 1970s, played recorded songs at different times of day and reported that a song broadcast at dawn could be detected up to twice as far away as the same song at midday. However, later studies in other habitats produced mixed results. Critics also pointed out that if sound transmission were the main factor, birds ought to sing just as intensely at dusk, when conditions are often similar. Few of them do.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second idea concerns food rather than sound. Many songbirds feed on insects, and in the dim light before sunrise their prey is both hard to see and relatively inactive in the cold. According to this view, argued most forcefully by the behavioural ecologist Tomás Ibarra, the early morning is simply a poor time to search for food, so a bird loses little by singing instead. Once the light improves and the air warms, it becomes more profitable to stop singing and start foraging. Ibarra points to his own observations of warblers in northern Spain, which suggest that the chorus ends almost exactly when the light becomes strong enough for efficient hunting.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other researchers regard the chorus as a form of advertisement. A small bird may lose up to a tenth of its body weight during a cold night, simply keeping warm. A male that sings vigorously at dawn is therefore demonstrating that he has come through the night with energy to spare, a message that rivals and potential mates cannot easily fake. Experiments by the Kessler Research Group in Austria appeared to support this idea: when wild great tits were given extra food the previous evening, they began singing earlier and sang for longer the next morning. Yet the same group noted that the effect was modest, and that birds which received no extra food still sang at length. Energy reserves, they concluded, are only part of the story.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A fourth explanation looks instead at the social lives of birds. In many species, a female lays her eggs early in the morning and is thought to be most fertile shortly afterwards. A male who sings loudly at this time may be guarding his partner, warning other males to keep away when the risk of a rival mating with her is greatest. The field biologist Ruth Adeyemi adds a further, territorial dimension. In her view, the chorus works as a kind of daily roll call: each male announces that he is still alive and still in possession of his territory. A male whose neighbour falls silent can quickly move to claim the vacant ground, so remaining quiet at dawn carries a real risk.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In recent years, towns and cities have provided researchers with an unplanned experiment. Street lighting means that urban birds experience something like daybreak long before the sun rises, and morning traffic noise can drown out songs once the rush hour begins. A study led by Dr Paolo Ricci in Milan found that blackbirds living near bright street lamps began their song up to an hour earlier than those in darker parks, and that birds in noisy districts started earlier still. For Ricci, the second finding suggests that birds are trying to be heard before traffic noise makes communication difficult, which supports the importance of sound transmission. The first, however, implies that timing is also linked to light levels, which fits Ibarra's argument. His conclusion is that the chorus is probably shaped by several pressures at once, and that their relative importance differs from one species to another.

groups.instructions:
Complete the sentences below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in the gaps.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted, blasting millions of tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. There the gas formed a fine haze of sulphate particles that reflected a small fraction of incoming sunlight back into space, and over the following year average global temperatures fell by roughly half a degree Celsius. For a number of scientists, the episode raised a tantalising possibility: if a volcano could cool the planet by accident, perhaps humans could do so deliberately. The proposal that grew out of this thought, known as stratospheric aerosol injection, would involve high-altitude aircraft releasing reflective particles into the upper atmosphere. Within two decades it has travelled from the fringes of climate science to the agendas of respected research bodies. That shift is understandable, but I shall argue that much of the enthusiasm surrounding it rests on a misunderstanding of what the technique can and cannot achieve.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The attraction is easy to see. Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is slow, expensive and politically fraught, and even if emissions stopped tomorrow, the carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere would go on warming the planet for decades. Aerosol injection, by contrast, promises results within months, at a cost that some estimates put at a few billion dollars a year, a trivial sum when set against the damage caused by heatwaves, droughts and failed harvests. The atmospheric physicist Daniel Moreau has gone so far as to call it 'the only lever we have that works on a human timescale'. It would be dishonest to dismiss this case out of hand. The speed and cheapness of the approach are real advantages, and anyone who opposes it must take them seriously.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that aerosols treat a symptom rather than the disease. They would lower temperatures, but they would do nothing to slow the build-up of carbon dioxide itself, nor to stop the oceans from growing more acidic as they absorb it, a change that threatens corals and shellfish however cool the water may be. Moreover, the particles drift out of the stratosphere within a year or two, so they would have to be replenished continuously, perhaps for a century or more. If injection were ever halted abruptly, whether because of war, economic collapse or political disagreement, the warming it had been masking would return within a few years, far faster than ecosystems or societies could adapt. Climate scientists call this 'termination shock', and in my view it is the most serious objection to the whole enterprise, because it would bind future generations to a programme they never chose.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second problem concerns fairness. Global average temperature is a convenient figure, but nobody actually lives in the global average. Simulations run at the Nordhavn Climate Centre suggest that reflecting sunlight would alter rainfall unevenly, possibly weakening the monsoons on which hundreds of millions of farmers in South Asia and West Africa depend. Other models are less pessimistic, and the honest answer is that no one yet knows. But that uncertainty is precisely the point. A technology whose regional effects cannot be predicted, and which a single wealthy nation could deploy on its own, raises questions of governance that existing international institutions are simply not equipped to answer.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Opponents frequently add a third argument, often described as 'moral hazard': the fear that the mere prospect of a technological fix will weaken the determination to cut emissions. I find this argument less convincing than its supporters suppose. Surveys conducted by the sociologist Ingrid Halvorsen found that members of the public who learned about geoengineering became, if anything, slightly more worried about climate change, not less. The real risk lies elsewhere. It is not ordinary citizens who are likely to relax, but governments and industries already searching for reasons to delay, who may seize on the idea as a convenient excuse. That is a political danger rather than a psychological one, and it must be met with political rather than scientific answers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that research should stop. Some campaigners have called for an international ban not only on deployment but on outdoor experiments of any kind. This seems to me mistaken. If the climate warms faster than expected, future leaders may come under intense pressure to attempt aerosol injection, and it would be far better for them to decide on the basis of careful evidence than in a state of panic. Small, openly reported field trials, supervised by bodies that include representatives of the countries most at risk, would allow scientists to test their predictions without committing anyone to deployment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What research must never become is an alibi. At best, solar geoengineering might buy time in which to cut emissions and draw carbon out of the air; it cannot replace either effort. Describing it as a form of insurance is reasonable only if we remember what insurance is for. It reduces the cost of a disaster, but it is no reason to drive more recklessly. The technology deserves careful study. It does not yet deserve our hopes.
